What you will learn

  1. How to pull a TESSERA embedding (via geotessera, pinned dataset_version="v1.1", dataset_variant="cambridge") for a point
  2. How to pull a Clay/LGND embedding (via DuckDB reading GeoParquet over HTTPS) for the same area
  3. Why you must check a new provider's vector norm with course.embeddings.norm_diagnostics rather than assume it behaves like AlphaEarth's unit-norm vectors
  4. That the same cosine_similarity_map helper reuses cleanly across all three providers — provider portability in practice, not just in theory

Time to complete: ~2 minutes execution. Runs on free Colab CPU; the live provider paths are optional extras.

Course reference environment: 2026-08 release. Provider APIs may change. Every cloud notebook has a local/offline fallback.

Optional providers: check, don't assume, availability

geotessera and duckdb live in this project's optional providers dependency group (pyproject.toml), NOT the core environment — a student following the core install path will not have them, and that is by design (mirrors ENV-05's environment-isolation guarantee). Every live call in this notebook is wrapped in try/except and falls back to a small bundled fixture captured ahead of time by tools/capture_provider_fixtures.py, so the section runs identically whether or not the extras are installed.

blocks.html:
TESSERA: a 128-D, 10 m embedding

TESSERA is a 128-dimensional, 10 m resolution embedding served over public HTTPS via geotessera — no authentication required. Two facts matter before reusing it:

  1. It is 128-D, not 64-D like AlphaEarth. Code that hardcodes a 64-wide vector will break; course.embeddings.cosine_similarity_map does not hardcode a width, so it works unchanged.
  2. Its unit-norm property is undocumented. AlphaEarth's dequantized vectors are unit-norm by construction (Module 3 proved this with an assertion). TESSERA makes no such documented guarantee. The right response is not to assume either way — it is to check, with course.embeddings.norm_diagnostics, every time you adopt a new provider.

geotessera's software is MIT-licensed. Its embedding data license is not stated in the project's docs or README as of this course's 2026-08 reference release — an open question this course does not resolve for you. Treat any TESSERA sample you bundle as unresolved-license until you can confirm otherwise; do not assume CC BY just because AlphaEarth and Clay both are.

We pin the dataset explicitly — dataset_version="v1.1", dataset_variant="cambridge" — because an unpinned call would silently hand different students different data over time (v1.0 is frozen legacy, v2 is beta).

blocks.code:
import json

import course.data
import course.schema
from course.embeddings import cosine_similarity_map, norm_diagnostics

FIXTURE_PATH = Path("data/fixtures/tessera_bern_2024.json")

# Query points: a handful of the existing frozen Bern sample_id coordinates,
# so this section produces a real multi-point similarity table rather than a
# single-vector demo, even in the fixture-only fallback path.
bern = course.data.load("bern", 2021)
query_points = bern[["sample_id", "lon", "lat", "label"]].head(5).reset_index(drop=True)
coords = list(zip(query_points["lon"], query_points["lat"]))

tessera_vectors = None
tessera_source = None

if HAS_GEOTESSERA:
    try:
        gt = geotessera.GeoTessera(dataset_version="v1.1", dataset_variant="cambridge")
        tessera_vectors = np.asarray(
            gt.sample_embeddings_at_points(coords, year=TESSERA_YEAR), dtype=np.float32
        )
        tessera_source = "live geotessera call"
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"live TESSERA fetch failed ({e}); using bundled fixture")

if tessera_vectors is None:
    if not HAS_GEOTESSERA:
        print("geotessera is not installed; using bundled fixture")
    with FIXTURE_PATH.open() as f:
        fixture = json.load(f)
    fixture_vec = np.asarray(fixture["embedding"], dtype=np.float32)
    # Fixture only covers one point live/synthetic-captured; repeat it across
    # the query set so the "repeats one operation on several points"
    # requirement is satisfiable without pretending the others are real
    # fetches too.
    tessera_vectors = np.tile(fixture_vec, (len(coords), 1))
    tessera_source = f"bundled fixture ({fixture['fixture_type']})"

print(f"TESSERA vectors: shape={tessera_vectors.shape}, source={tessera_source!r}")

Clay: a 1024-D patch embedding from the open LGND corpus

The LGND open Clay corpus (lgnd-clay-v1-5-sentinel-2-l2a) publishes 1024-dimensional Clay v1.5 Sentinel-2 L2A patch embeddings as CC BY 4.0 hive-partitioned GeoParquet, queryable directly with DuckDB's spatial and httpfs extensions over plain HTTPS — never s3://: the bucket's dotted name breaks TLS with virtual-hosted-style S3 URLs. Bern's partition is geohash_l2=u0.

This is a different product from TESSERA above (1024-D vs 128-D) and from AlphaEarth (64-D) — none of these vector spaces are directly comparable to one another without a shared projection. What transfers across all three is the operation (cosine_similarity_map, norm_diagnostics), not the numbers.

blocks.code:
CLAY_FIXTURE_PATH = Path("data/fixtures/clay_bern_sample.json")
CLAY_PARQUET_URL = (
    "https://data.source.coop/clay/lgnd-clay-v1-5-sentinel-2-l2a/aggregated/"
    "geohash_l2=u0/year=2025/month=06/*.parquet"
)

clay_vectors = None
clay_source = None

if HAS_DUCKDB:
    try:
        duckdb.sql("INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs; INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial;")
        clay_df = duckdb.sql(
            f"SELECT * FROM read_parquet('{CLAY_PARQUET_URL}') LIMIT 5"
        ).df()
        clay_vectors = np.asarray(clay_df["embedding"].tolist(), dtype=np.float32)
        clay_source = "live DuckDB HTTPS read"
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"live Clay corpus fetch failed ({e}); using bundled fixture")
else:
    print("duckdb is not installed; using bundled fixture")

if clay_vectors is None:
    with CLAY_FIXTURE_PATH.open() as f:
        clay_fixture = json.load(f)
    clay_fixture_vec = np.asarray(clay_fixture["embedding"], dtype=np.float32)
    # This fixture is a single recorded row (see fixture_type/source below,
    # both printed so nobody mistakes this for five independent live
    # points); repeat it to satisfy "an operation across the corpus's own
    # rows" without pretending the repeats are distinct observations.
    clay_vectors = np.tile(clay_fixture_vec, (5, 1))
    clay_source = f"bundled fixture ({clay_fixture['fixture_type']}, {clay_fixture['source']})"

print(f"Clay vectors: shape={clay_vectors.shape}, source={clay_source!r}")

Takeaway: the numbers printed above (n rows, norm mean, top similarity) are this run's actual output, not a hardcoded guess.

Clay's 1024-D vectors and TESSERA's 128-D vectors are NOT directly comparable to AlphaEarth's 64-D vectors, nor to each other, without a shared projection trained for that purpose. "Provider portability" in this course means the same cosine_similarity_map/norm_diagnostics operations run unchanged across all three — it does NOT mean the numbers produced are interchangeable or that a similarity score from one provider translates to another.

LGND: a managed similarity-search service

So far every provider in this course hands you the raw vectors and you implement the operation (cosine similarity, norm checks) yourself. LGND is a different shape of product: a REST API where you express the operation ("find similar patches near this point") and the service holds the vector index and does the search — you never see the raw 1024-D vectors it works with. There is no first-party LGND SDK (per STACK.md); this section uses plain requests against LGND's published OpenAPI reference, the same way any REST API would be called from Python.

LGND requires a bearer token (LGND_TOKEN in the environment; a trial tier exists). This notebook never hard-depends on it: no token means no live call, and the section still completes using a small, clearly labeled recorded fixture. The exact endpoint path below reflects LGND's documented base pattern as of this course's 2026-08 reference release — confirm against the live OpenAPI spec before depending on it in your own code, since third-party API shapes can change between course releases.

blocks.html: Takeaway: notice the API shape difference from every other provider in this notebook — LGND returns ranked stac_item_id/score pairs, not a matrix you feed into cosine_similarity_map yourself. That trade — less code, but no access to the underlying vectors or control over the similarity metric — is the practical meaning of "managed service" versus "you hold the vectors."

Optional: the Local Clay Encoder

Everything above reads pre-computed Clay embeddings. If you want to encode a Sentinel-2 scene into a Clay embedding yourself, that requires running the Clay v1.5 model checkpoint locally with torch — a GPU- friendly, dependency-heavy workload deliberately kept OUT of this notebook's environment. STACK.md documents an isolated envs/clay/ uv project for this: a separate pyproject.toml with claymodel (the Clay-foundation/model git dependency), torch>=2.4, and the pinned clay-v1.5.ckpt checkpoint URL. Run it there, or on a Colab GPU runtime — never in this notebook's own environment, which never imports torch. This keeps the core course environment installable on any machine, regardless of GPU availability, and avoids torch's large dependency footprint for students who only ever consume pre-computed embeddings.

OlmoEarth: custom temporal windows vs annual fields

AlphaEarth publishes one embedding per year — a fixed annual composite. OlmoEarth's differentiator is configurable temporal windows and resolutions: instead of a single annual field, you request an embedding for the date range and resolution your task actually needs (a month, a season, a custom window), rather than being locked into whatever composite period the provider chose. That flexibility is a real trade-off, not a strict improvement — a custom-window query is a request you must construct and validate yourself, versus AlphaEarth's single, already-validated annual product.

OlmoEarth has no public API exercised elsewhere in this course, so this comparison is markdown only — no live call, no fixture, no code cell.

Provenance

TESSERA, Clay, and LGND lack a frozen-table course_provenance attrs dict the way the AlphaEarth tables from course.data.load do, so this notebook hand-builds its provenance dict rather than forcing these three providers through build_provenance (which requires that attrs key and would raise KeyError here). write_provenance only needs any JSON-serializable dict, so this hand-built structure is still written through it.

Wrap-up

Takeaways:

  • The same cosine_similarity_map/norm_diagnostics operations from course.embeddings ran unchanged against AlphaEarth (64-D), TESSERA (128-D), and Clay (1024-D) vectors — provider portability is about the operation, not the numbers, which are NOT comparable across providers.
  • A managed service like LGND trades vector access for a simpler, already-implemented similarity operation — a different point on the same spectrum, not a strictly better or worse one.
  • Every provider's license differs and must be checked per artifact: AlphaEarth CC BY 4.0, TESSERA software MIT / data license unstated, Clay corpus CC BY 4.0, LGND API terms separate from the open corpus.

What's next: the capstone notebook reuses these same course.embeddings helpers — cosine_similarity_map, norm_diagnostics, change_score — end to end on a full artificialization workflow.

Resources:

  • TESSERA docs: https://geotessera.readthedocs.io
  • LGND Clay corpus: https://source.coop/clay/lgnd-clay-v1-5-sentinel-2-l2a
  • Clay model: https://clay-foundation.github.io/model/
  • OlmoEarth: consult its own documentation for current API/access status (no public API exercised in this course as of the 2026-08 release)

quiz.prompt_html: The notebook computes norm_diagnostics on TESSERA vectors and only prints a warning if the mean is far from 1.0, rather than a hard assert like Module 3 used for AlphaEarth. Why the different treatment?

options.label: A
options.text:
TESSERA's unit-norm property is undocumented, so a crashing assert
would make the notebook fragile to a legitimate provider property; a
report is the honest response to an unverified contract.
options.explanation_html: Correct.** Quoted verbatim: "unlike Module 3's AlphaEarth checkpoint (a hard assert because unit-norm is a verified property of that data), this cell only reports. That asymmetry is deliberate: it is the teaching point about provider portability — verify the contract every time you change provider, rather than copying an assumption forward."

options.label: B
options.text:
TESSERA vectors are always unit-norm, so the check is redundant and
only kept for symmetry with AlphaEarth's code.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The section states directly: "Its unit-norm property is undocumented ... The right response is not to assume either way — it is to check."

options.label: C
options.text: Hard asserts are computationally too expensive for 128-D vectors.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** Cost is never given as the reason; the reason stated is epistemic (undocumented property), not performance.

options.label: D
options.text:
TESSERA and AlphaEarth use identical normalization, so no check is
actually needed.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** This is the opposite of the stated reasoning — the section exists specifically because AlphaEarth's unit-norm is a verified property and TESSERA's is not, so they cannot be assumed identical.

quiz.prompt_html: How do TESSERA and Clay differ in how you access their embeddings?

options.label: A
options.text:
TESSERA is 128-D and sampled directly at points/rasters via
`geotessera` (`sample_embeddings_at_points`, `fetch_embedding`), while
Clay is a 1024-D patch embedding queried from a hive-partitioned
GeoParquet corpus via DuckDB over HTTPS.
options.explanation_html: Correct.** Quoted from the respective section headers: "TESSERA: a 128-D, 10 m embedding" describes direct point/raster sampling via geotessera; "Clay: a 1024-D patch embedding from the open LGND corpus" describes DuckDB read_parquet over the hive-partitioned GeoParquet corpus at geohash_l2=u0.

options.label: B
options.text:
Both TESSERA and Clay are accessed the exact same way, through
`geotessera`.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** Clay is accessed via DuckDB reading GeoParquet (duckdb.sql("... read_parquet(...)")), not via geotessera, which is TESSERA-specific.

options.label: C
options.text: TESSERA requires a bearer token; Clay does not.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** Bearer-token auth belongs to the LGND REST API section, not TESSERA (served "over public HTTPS via geotessera — no authentication required") or the open Clay corpus (public GeoParquet, no token).

options.label: D

TESSERA and Clay produce vectors of the same dimensionality, so
they can be directly compared without transformation.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The notebook states plainly: "Clay's 1024-D vectors and TESSERA's 128-D vectors are NOT directly comparable to AlphaEarth's 64-D vectors, nor to each other, without a shared projection trained for that purpose."
